docs.title: Vault
docs.text:
Vault is a backup and restore daemon for Unraid servers. It protects Docker containers, libvirt VMs, ZFS datasets, folders, and plugins by backing them up to pluggable storage destinations — local disk, SFTP, SMB, NFS, WebDAV, or S3-compatible object storage. Vault ships with a REST API, an MCP server for AI assistants, WebSocket progress streaming, and an integrated web UI built with Svelte 5.

Get started →

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text:
• Back up more than containers — Docker containers, libvirt VMs, ZFS datasets, folders, and installed Unraid plugins.
  • Send backups anywhere — local disk, SFTP, SMB, NFS, WebDAV, or S3-compatible object storage, with per-destination bandwidth throttling.
  • Choose a strategy — full, incremental, and differential chains with simple-count or Long-Term Retention.
  • Stay safe — backups encrypted with your backup password (age encryption — a modern, audited standard), content-defined deduplication, and per-run SHA-256 verification.
  • Monitor in real time — live WebSocket progress streaming across Dashboard, Jobs, Restore, Storage, History, Replication, Recovery, Logs, and Settings pages.

See How Backup Works for the concepts behind these features.

docs.title: Finding your way
docs.text:
• New to Vault? Getting Started walks you from install to your first backup in about ten minutes.
  • Setting things up? The Guides are step-by-step recipes for jobs, storage, anomaly detection, and disaster recovery.
  • Curious how it works? How Backup Works explains full/incremental chains, retention, encryption, and deduplication in plain language.
  • Automating? See the REST API and MCP server.

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text:
• Home Assistant — monitor jobs and trigger backups from your dashboard with the ready-to-use custom integration ha-vault.
  • AI assistants (MCP) — drive Vault from Claude and other MCP clients via the built-in MCP server.
  • Scripting & automation — the full REST API exposes jobs, storage, runs, and restore points.

docs.title: Support Vault
docs.text:
Vault is free and open source, built and maintained in my own time. If it protects something you care about, sponsoring on GitHub helps keep it maintained — new features, Unraid compatibility as it evolves, and support for the people using it.

Not in a position to sponsor? Starring the repository, reporting bugs, and sharing Vault with other Unraid users all help just as much.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
Base URL: http://<host>:24085/api/v1

The Vault daemon exposes a REST API for managing backups, storage destinations, and system settings. WebSocket events are available for real-time progress streaming.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
By default Vault binds to 127.0.0.1 and all loopback requests are unauthenticated. When you configure an API key under Settings → Security → API Access, remote requests (non-loopback IPs) must include the key in every request:

X-API-Key: <your-api-key>

Loopback requests (127.0.0.1 and ::1) are always exempt from API key validation so that the Unraid plugin proxy can reach the daemon without a key.

Generating a key: Go to Settings → Security → API Access → Generate Key. Copy and store it securely — it is shown only once. Use this key for Home Assistant, replication targets, and any other external integrations.

docs.title: Jobs
docs.text:
The job payload's backup_type_chain field accepts full, incremental, or differential. Incremental and differential jobs automatically run as a full backup on their first run (when the job has no previous restore point to attach to); later runs capture only changes.

docs.title: Restoring the database (restore-db)
docs.text:
POST /storage/{id}/restore-db takes a JSON body:

  • storage_path — path of the database backup on the destination, e.g. _vault/vault.db.latest.age (encrypted) or a timestamped copy like _vault/vault.db.2026-07-01T02-00-00.age. Unencrypted backups use the .db extension.
  • passphrase — the backup password; required when the backup is encrypted.
  • verify_only — when true, validates the backup (and passphrase) without replacing the current database.

List the available backups first with GET /storage/{id}/db-backups.

docs.title: MCP (Model Context Protocol)
docs.text:
Method Endpoint Description Any /mcp Streamable-HTTP MCP entry point (Claude Desktop, web AI clients). Daemon mode only. Any /mcp/* MCP transport sub-paths used by the protocol

See MCP Integration for the available tools and client configuration.

docs.title: WebSocket
docs.text:
Connect to /api/v1/ws for real-time event streaming. Events include:

  • progress — per-item backup/restore progress with bytes-done and rate
  • job_state — backup or restore lifecycle transitions
  • runner_queue — current and queued jobs
  • config_changed — emitted after any CRUD mutation (jobs, storage, settings, replication) so dashboards refresh derived state
  • import_completed — emitted after a successful Storage → Import run

Origin patterns cover localhost, 127.0.0.1, *.local, 192.168.*.*, 10.*.*.*, and the full RFC 1918 172.16.0.0/12 range (including Docker's default 172.17.0.0/16).

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
This page is for developers and contributors — it describes Vault's internal design. If you just want to use Vault, start with Getting Started.

Vault is a single Go binary that runs as a daemon on Unraid servers. It provides backup and restore for Docker containers, libvirt VMs, ZFS datasets, folders, and plugins.

docs.title: Layered Design
docs.text:
CLI (Cobra) -> API Server (Chi + WebSocket Hub) -> Handlers -> DB / Storage / Engine / Runner
Layer Package Description CLI internal/cli/ Cobra commands: vault daemon, vault replica, vault mcp, vault dedup API internal/api/ Chi router, REST handlers, WebSocket integration MCP internal/mcp/ Model Context Protocol tools over streamable HTTP and stdio Database internal/db/ SQLite (WAL, pure-Go driver) with hybrid snapshot + USB shadow Storage internal/storage/ Local, SFTP, SMB, NFS, WebDAV, and S3 adapters (factory-dispatched) Engine internal/engine/ Per-type backup/restore handlers (container, VM, ZFS, folder, plugin) Runner internal/runner/ Job orchestration, retention, verification, compression Dedup internal/dedup/ Keyed-FastCDC chunker, per-destination dedup repo, GC Crypto internal/crypto/ AES-256-GCM, server key, passphrase-derived data keys Replication internal/replication/ Pull-mode replication client + syncer Scheduler internal/scheduler/ Cron-based scheduling WebSocket internal/ws/ Real-time event hub for backup progress and config changes Notify internal/notify/ Unraid notifications + Discord webhooks Diagnostics internal/diagnostics/ Redacted ZIP bundle (system info, schema, runs, scheduler, daemon log) Logbuf internal/logbuf/ In-memory ring buffer that captures every log.* line for diagnostics

docs.title: storage.Adapter
docs.text:
type Adapter interface {
    Write(path string, reader io.Reader) error
    WriteFrom(path string, open func() (io.ReadCloser, error)) error
    Read(path string) (io.ReadCloser, error)
    ReadRange(path string, offset, length int64) (io.ReadCloser, error)
    Delete(path string) error
    List(prefix string) ([]FileInfo, error)
    Stat(path string) (FileInfo, error)
    TestConnection() error
    GetCapacity(ctx context.Context) (Capacity, error)
    Usage() (free, total int64, err error)
}

WriteFrom lets the retry layer re-issue a failed upload from a fresh stream; ReadRange serves the dedup layer's partial pack reads; GetCapacity and Usage feed the capacity widgets and trajectory detector.

Adapters that hold persistent resources (SFTP, SMB) implement io.Closer and are released by storage.CloseAdapter. Bandwidth throttling is layered on top via a RateLimit config field for every remote type. Adapters are constructed via storage.NewAdapter(type, configJSON).

docs.title: engine.Handler
docs.text:
type Handler interface {
    Backup(ctx context.Context, item BackupItem, dest string, progress ProgressFunc) (*BackupResult, error)
    Restore(ctx context.Context, item BackupItem, source string, progress ProgressFunc) error
    ListItems() ([]BackupItem, error)
}

Handlers that support content-defined chunking additionally implement engine.ChunkedHandler (BackupChunked / RestoreChunked) so the runner can route them through the dedup repo on dedup-enabled destinations.

docs.title: Build Tags
docs.text:
• vm.go, vm_restore.go, and other libvirt-touching files use //go:build linux — real libvirt RPC against /var/run/libvirt/libvirt-sock
  • vm_stub.go: //go:build !linux — stubs for macOS / Windows so the rest of the daemon still builds and tests run
  • ZFS (engine/zfs.go) calls out to the host zfs binary; the code itself is platform-neutral
  • Local builds and the full test suite work on macOS without libvirt installed

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
SQLite with WAL mode and busy timeout. Pure Go driver via modernc.org/sqlite (no CGO).

sql.Open("sqlite", path+"?_txlock=immediate&_pragma=busy_timeout(30000)&_pragma=journal_mode(WAL)&_pragma=foreign_keys(ON)&_pragma=journal_size_limit(67108864)")

Schema is applied inline at open time via CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS (no versioned migrations). Twelve tables: storage_destinations, jobs, job_items, job_runs, restore_points, settings, activity_log, verify_runs, replication_sources, dedup_packs, dedup_chunks, dedup_gc_runs.

docs.title: Hybrid snapshot layout
docs.text:
To survive Unraid's USB-backed boot (where writing every commit to flash would wear the drive), the daemon runs in hybrid mode by default:

  1. Working DB — /var/local/vault/vault.db (tmpfs-backed; fast, never written to flash directly)
  2. Primary snapshot — <discovered cache pool>/.vault/vault.db (periodic copies; the authoritative on-disk source)
  3. USB shadow — /boot/config/plugins/vault/vault.db.backup (refreshed after config changes via the SetConfigChangeHook pathway, so the flash copy stays current without per-row writes)

On startup the daemon restores from the freshest integrity-passing source among the primary snapshot, the default cache snapshot, rotated snapshot copies, the USB-direct live DB (written when a boot ran without a mounted pool), and the USB shadow — falling back to a fresh DB only if none pass. Freshness is compared by modification time so a boot that ran in USB-direct mode can never be silently reverted by an older cache snapshot on the next hybrid boot (issue #241). An emhttp event script (event/stopping_svcs) stops the daemon gracefully on array stop/reboot so the final flush completes, and event/started ensures the daemon is running once the array is up.

docs.text:
./build/vault daemon --db=vault.db --addr=:24085

Build constraints:

  • web/embed.go uses //go:embed dist/*, so web/dist must exist before go build (handled by make build-local and CI's web build step).
  • internal/release embeds CHANGELOG.md; the build flow first copies the repo-root changelog into internal/release/CHANGELOG.md before lint/tests/build (also mirrored by the Makefile and CI).

The production binary is built with CGO_ENABLED=0 using modernc.org/sqlite, keeping it pure Go.

docs.title: Unraid Plugin
docs.text:
Install via the Unraid Community Applications store, or paste the plugin URL into Plugins > Install Plugin:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ruaan-deysel/vault/main/plugin/vault.plg

The daemon runs at /usr/local/sbin/vault with the database at /boot/config/plugins/vault/vault.db.

Service management:

/etc/rc.d/rc.vault start
/etc/rc.d/rc.vault stop
/etc/rc.d/rc.vault restart
/etc/rc.d/rc.vault status

Uninstall removes runtime and configuration traces (including the database) while preserving backup data in configured storage destinations.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text: • Dedup GC is delete-only. Garbage collection removes packs whose every chunk is unreferenced. A pack with even one live chunk is kept; its dead bytes are reported as Reclaimable ("rewritable bytes") on the Storage card and persisted per GC run in dedup_gc_runs, but they are not yet physically reclaimed. Compaction/repacking is tracked in #103. This matches early borg/restic behaviour and is a deliberate v1 choice — small (24 MiB) packs bound the stranded space.

docs.title: Version
docs.text: Vault uses date-based versioning in the VERSION file with the format YYYY.MM.PATCH. Version is injected via ldflags at build time (-X main.version, -X main.buildDate, -X main.commit).

docs.title: Top-navigation quick link (Backups.page)
docs.text: plugin/pages/Backups.page is an optional top-nav entry (Menu="Tasks", Type="xmenu" — the same extension point Community Applications uses) gated by NAV_LINK in vault.cfg via its Cond header, toggled from the Vault settings page through control.php's navlink action. It embeds the SPA's proxy entrypoint (include/app.php) in an iframe sized to the viewport. Because app.php injects Unraid's CSRF token once per render and the SPA has no in-app refresh, the frame reloads itself when the tab regains visibility after >10 minutes hidden so write actions keep working across token rotations. In proxy mode the SPA polls; WebSocket-only live events do not stream here (matching the Utilities page).

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All notable changes to the Vault plugin will be documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project uses date-based versioning (YYYY.MM.PATCH).

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Replication targets now show what the last sync actually did. A target that connected but had nothing new to copy previously just read "Synced", which looked the same as a sync that transferred data — so replication could appear to "connect but not do much". Each target now shows an explicit Up to date state when a sync found nothing new, a per-sync summary (jobs synced, new restore points, bytes transferred, and any failures), and the time replication last fully succeeded. These counters are stored with each run, so they are visible on page load and after a refresh, not only in the moment a sync finishes. Closes #287.
  • Contributor build and run guidance is now discoverable from the repository root and docs site. Added explicit local development prerequisites and workflows across CONTRIBUTING.md, README.md, and docs pages so new contributors can find compile/build/run/lint/test/docker instructions, frontend-dev notes, and architecture links from a single entry path. Closes #341.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: • Updated Go and web dependencies to their latest compatible releases and resolved a high-severity advisory in the web nanoid dependency. gosec, govulncheck, and the Go linter pass clean, and the MCP integration remains on the go-sdk v1.7.0 API.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • A scheduled deep verify no longer piles onto a destination that a backup is still writing to. Deep verification streams and re-hashes every stored item, so running it against the same storage destination as an in-progress backup saturated the shared disk and network — the backup slowed to a crawl and looked frozen, with nothing in the logs to explain it. Vault now defers a scheduled deep verify while a backup is running on the same destination and records why in the activity log, letting the deep verify run at its next scheduled tick instead. Quick verification (existence and size checks only) is light enough to keep running alongside a backup, and an on-demand verify you trigger yourself is never deferred. Closes #290.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• A container's database dump is no longer lost when the restore does not reload it. When a restore left the SQL dump in place — because the restored volume was the newer, consistent copy, the container was not running, or the database never became ready — the dump only ever existed in a temporary staging directory that Vault cleaned up when the restore finished, so there was nothing left for an operator to find. Vault now copies the un-reloaded dump to a durable, discoverable location and reports the exact path in the restore progress and logs: the custom restore destination when one is set (<destination>/<container>-database.sql), otherwise beside the container's first restored volume (for example /mnt/user/appdata/<container>-database.sql). The file name is prefixed with the container name so restores that share a parent directory do not collide, and the container backup guide now documents where the dump lands for in-place and custom restores. Closes #289.
  • The web console no longer gets stuck on an endless "connecting" screen after a plugin upgrade until you clear site data. The page that the Unraid shortcut opens (app.php) served the app shell with no cache headers, so a browser — Brave especially — could keep a copy of it from before an upgrade. That stale shell still pointed at the previous JavaScript bundles, which the upgrade had replaced with new content-hashed filenames, so the browser fetched bundles that no longer existed and the app never finished loading. The shell is now sent with the same "never cache" policy the daemon already applies to its own index.html, so every visit loads the shell that matches the installed version. Closes #288.
  • The Dashboard "Largest backups" tile no longer shrinks after incremental backups run. It was computed from only the last handful of runs, so once a job's large full backup dropped out of that short window the tile fell back to the size of the most recent — much smaller — incremental. It now reads the largest backup per job from the latest 200 history records, so the full backup remains represented well beyond the short recent-runs window. Closes #286.
  • A custom restore location is now honoured when restoring a plugin from a deduplicated destination. The deduplicated plugin restore only looked at the restore directory passed to it directly and ignored the restore_destination setting as a fallback, unlike the container restore path which already checks both. In current use both are set to the same value so there was no visible effect, but the two independent paths could have drifted apart in future. The plugin restore now falls back to the setting when no directory is passed, keeping the two in step. Closes #274.
  • A plugin backed up to a deduplicated destination now keeps its .plg installer file. The deduplicated plugin backup only stored the plugin's config directory, leaving out the .plg installer at /boot/config/plugins/<name>.plg. A restore from such a backup — for example onto a fresh Unraid install — brought the configuration back but not the installer, so Unraid might not recognise the plugin on the next boot. The .plg is now stored alongside the config in the same restore point and written back on restore, matching what the non-deduplicated plugin backup already did. Backups taken before this change simply have no installer to restore, exactly as before. Closes #273.
  • Restoring selected files from a plugin backup on a deduplicated destination no longer restores the whole plugin. When a plugin backup lived on a dedup destination and you picked specific files to restore, the file-picker selection was dropped on the way through the deduplicated restore path and the entire plugin config directory was written back instead. The selection now carries through to the folder restore that reconstructs the files, so only the chosen files are restored — matching how the same picker already worked for non-dedup plugin restores. Closes #271.
  • Backup sizes now read the same everywhere they are shown. Four operator-facing places still formatted sizes with their own math instead of the shared byte contract, so the same backup could read differently depending on where you looked: the Storage page's saved-backups list stopped at TB with no clamp (a petabyte showed as 1024.0 TB), the Recover Vault wizard always printed raw kilobytes (1048576 KB for a gigabyte), the packaged plugin History page always printed megabytes (1073741824.0 MB for a petabyte), and the transfer-speed label capped at GB/s and disagreed with the app near unit boundaries. All four now go through the same formatBytes contract the app and notifications already use, so a size or speed reads identically across the console, the wizard, the plugin pages, and Discord/webhook messages. Closes #270.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Database containers can now be backed up as a proper database dump, not just its files. PostgreSQL, MySQL, and MariaDB containers get an optional "Also save a … dump" tick in the job editor. Vault exports the databases with the server running and stores the dump alongside the usual file backup — copying a database's files while it is writing can capture a torn state that will not load, whereas a dump is always consistent and can be reloaded into a different server version. The dump covers the whole server including users and permissions, so a restore does not come back missing the accounts the application signs in with. It uses the credentials already set on the container, so there is nothing to configure and no second copy of a password for you to look after. If the container exposes no usable root password, the dump is scoped to the database named in its environment instead, since an application user cannot read the whole server. A container that is stopped or stuck restarting is reported plainly rather than silently skipped.

Restoring puts the folders back and leaves the dump alongside them for you to reload by hand or into a different server version. It is deliberately not replayed over the restored folders: the dump is taken while the server is still running, the folders are copied after it stops, so the folders are the newer copy — and a reload would drop anything written while the dump was still being taken. Where the folders were read from a running server, and so may be mid-write, the dump is the trustworthy copy and is reloaded automatically; if that reload fails the restore fails with it, rather than handing back a database that looks restored and is not. Off unless you tick it. Closes #259.

  • Exclude the same paths everywhere, without editing every job. Settings → Backup Exclusions takes a list of paths that every folder and container backup skips. They are added to whatever a job already excludes rather than replacing it, so a job can still exclude more of its own. Useful for the paths that are never worth backing up anywhere — caches, sockets, scratch directories. Closes #257.
  • Containers can declare their own exclusions with a Docker label. Setting vault.exclude=/config/cache,/tmp on a container tells Vault to skip those paths when backing it up. The exclusions travel with the container, so a template or compose file carries its own answer and adding the container to a job needs no further setup. The paths are matched exactly like ones typed into the job wizard, and the job editor shows which mounts a label is skipping. A label can exclude paths but not the whole container — a catch-all pattern is refused, since the label is written by whoever built the image rather than by the person who owns the backup. On by default; it can be turned off in Settings → Backup Exclusions. Closes #258.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• A container backup now fails instead of quietly saving nothing when every one of its folders is excluded. With a broad exclusion rule — from the global list or a container's own label — it was possible for every backup-eligible folder to be skipped, leaving a backup that reported success but held only the container's configuration. It now stops with an error naming where to look, matching how virtual-machine backups already refuse to run when a VM has no disks they can handle. This applies to deduplicated destinations as well as ordinary ones: the check originally guarded only the ordinary path, so a dedup destination could still record a restore point holding no folder data at all — one that retention might later keep in place of a complete one. The check also runs before the container is stopped, so a backup that cannot produce anything no longer costs it any downtime.
  • Large backups to a dedup destination no longer slow to a crawl and appear frozen. Every time a backup finished a 24 MiB pack, Vault listed the entire _vault/index/ directory on the destination to work out the next index-blob number. That directory gains one entry per pack, so the cost grew with every pack written: a 500 GB folder flushes roughly 21,000 packs and so issued 21,000 listings of a directory holding up to 21,000 entries — hundreds of millions of directory entries pulled across the network in a single run. Progress crawled, got steadily worse the longer a backup ran, and on a remote destination (WebDAV/SFTP/S3) eventually degenerated into connection and DNS timeouts that failed the run. Vault now reads that directory once per backup and counts on from there, so index bookkeeping costs the same on the last pack as on the first. Existing destinations are picked up as-is — no re-upload, repair, or reconfiguration is needed. Closes #256.
  • A slow or stalled browser can no longer hold up a running backup. Live progress events were handed to the WebSocket layer with a blocking send, so once the outbound queue filled — a browser tab left open that had stopped reading, or a flaky connection — the backup goroutine itself waited on it. Progress updates are now discarded rather than queued when a connection cannot keep up, since the next update carries the same information. Events the interface cannot recover by waiting — run completion, item failures, queue changes — are still delivered reliably, so a busy backup never leaves a finished job showing as still running.
  • Backup runs no longer log a spurious "malformed settings JSON" warning. A job item saved without any per-item settings stored an empty value rather than an empty set, so every run that checked it reported the item as corrupt in the log. Nothing was actually wrong and backups were unaffected, but the warning pointed at a healthy item. Items now always store a valid value, and existing ones are read correctly without the warning. Genuinely corrupt settings are still reported.
  • A VM that ignores the request to shut down no longer fails the backup. Cold VM backups ask the guest to shut down gracefully and wait for it. If the guest accepted the request but never acted on it — no ACPI handler installed, sitting at a login prompt, or an application blocking shutdown — the wait timed out and the backup gave up with "waiting for domain … to shut off: timed out with state running", even though Vault already had a forced-stop step ready for exactly this situation. It now falls through to that forced stop, so a stubborn guest is powered off and the backup proceeds. A backup you cancel yourself is still never turned into a forced power-off. The same fix applies when a restore has to stop an existing VM before replacing it. Reported in #255.
  • "No space left on device" now explains itself on an Unraid user share. A backup writing to a path under /mnt/user could fail with a bare out-of-space error while the array showed terabytes free, which reads like a permissions fault or a Vault bug. It is neither: a user share spreads its contents across disks, but any single file is written to one of them, so a large VM disk image fails as soon as the disk it landed on is full — no matter what the array total says. The error now names the directory that filled and, for a user share, explains this and points at the settings that govern it (the share's Minimum Free Space and Split Level), or suggests targeting a specific disk or pool such as /mnt/cache instead. Reported in #255.
  • A dedup backup can no longer report success while leaving data that a later repair would discard. After writing a pack of deduplicated data, Vault recorded it in its local database before writing the matching record to the destination. If the second write failed, the backup still completed successfully, but the destination held data with no record of what was in it — so vault dedup repair, the tool for rebuilding the local database from the destination, would quietly drop it and reveal the backup had been unrestorable all along. The destination record is now written first, so a failure fails the backup immediately and visibly instead of surfacing later as missing data.
  • A backup can no longer be built on top of data that space reclamation has already marked for deletion. When reclaiming space, Vault records its intent to remove a pack before deleting it, so an interrupted run can be finished later. If the deletion itself failed — a destination that is reachable but refusing deletes, for instance — the pack's contents stayed listed as available, so the next backup of the same files would reuse them instead of storing its own copy. That backup then depended on data already marked for removal, and repairing the index afterwards would drop it, leaving the backup unrestorable. Contents of a pack marked for deletion are now excluded from reuse the moment that mark is recorded, while the record itself is kept so the next reclamation retries the delete. The affected backup simply stores its own copy instead. Existing destinations pick this up automatically on upgrade.
  • Repairing a dedup index can no longer lose chunks that a surviving pack still holds. vault dedup repair rebuilds the index by replaying the bookkeeping records stored alongside your backups, and it applied deletion records as it went. Because a chunk is recorded once and space reclamation copies chunks into a replacement pack before retiring the old one, replaying the retired pack's record last left the chunk attributed to it — and applying the deletion then removed the chunk outright, even though the replacement pack still held the data. Restores after a repair could then fail with missing chunks. The rebuild now determines which packs were retired before it replays anything, so the result no longer depends on record ordering. This only affected repair and disaster recovery; normal backups and restores were never at risk.
  • The interface now recovers on its own after losing contact with the daemon. A browser that stopped keeping up — a background tab, a flaky link — was disconnected by the daemon, and any update in flight at that moment was lost. Since a job's completion notice is what clears the progress display, losing that one message left a finished backup shown as still running until the page was reloaded. On reconnecting, the console now re-reads the current run state and reconciles what it missed, so the display corrects itself. The daemon also states plainly that it dropped a connection for falling behind, instead of closing it in a way indistinguishable from a network failure.
  • Per-file progress updates are now rate-limited to roughly one per second. Chunked backups and restores sent a WebSocket event for every single file — 46,000 events for a large music library — each one costing CPU on the server and work in the browser, for updates far faster than anyone can read. Backup, restore, and the restore download phase now report at a steady cadence instead. On-screen progress is unchanged in practice, and the internal stall detector still sees every file and every byte, so a genuinely hung backup is still detected just as quickly.
  • Restoring a differential or incremental container from a dedup destination no longer fails with "no such file or directory". Only the full backup would restore; every later point in the chain stopped with an error naming a directory that does not exist. Dedup backups keep their data in the chunk store rather than in a folder per container, but container restores were being sent down the older path that looks for that folder — a shortcut for restoring a single point directly was in place but sat behind a check that only folders ever reached. Container and plugin backups write a complete record of the item on every run, exactly as folders do, so restoring the chosen point on its own reproduces it correctly. Restores from non-dedup destinations are unchanged. Closes #266.
  • Saving a job in Batch container mode no longer fails with "invalid container_mode". Choosing Batch in the job editor and clicking Save returned an error and refused to save; Sequential saved normally. The job wizard, the backup runner and the rest of the codebase all call this mode stop_all, but the API's list of accepted values had been written as all_at_once — a name nothing else used — so the one value the interface could actually send was the one value the API rejected. Batch mode was therefore impossible to select on any job. The list now matches the rest of the stack. Any job still holding the old value — it could only have been written by the MCP interface, an import or a replication sync, none of which check this field — is converted once, on upgrade, so every such job changes together rather than only the ones that happen to get edited. Those jobs had been running sequentially despite the name, and will now genuinely stop all their containers together. Closes #261.
  • A cold VM backup no longer fails outright and leaves the guest powered off when the guest is slow to stop. Vault asked the guest to shut down and then waited for it, but treated "shutting down" — a passing state on the way to being off, while the guest is still running — as though the guest had already stopped. When a poll happened to land in that window, the backup pressed straight on to start its temporary session and libvirt refused with "domain is already running", so the backup failed while the guest carried on shutting down and stayed off. Because it depended on the timing of a single poll it struck only sometimes, which made it look like a random failure rather than a bug. Vault now waits for the guest to be genuinely off. Reported in #265.
  • A cold VM backup can no longer leave the guest powered off and the job stuck on "running" for hours. After a cold backup stopped a VM and copied its disks, the temporary paused session had to be torn down before the guest was started again. If that teardown failed, Vault returned immediately and never issued the start — so the VM stayed down, the run never finished, the job showed "running" indefinitely, and only restarting the daemon cleared it. The guest is now brought back up whether or not the teardown succeeded, and is resumed rather than restarted when the session is still paused, since a paused guest is just as unavailable as a stopped one. Both failures are reported instead of one hiding the other.
  • A backup that stops responding is now reported as stalled instead of sitting silently on "running". Several problems combined to make a wedged run invisible. The stall watchdog stopped running the moment it cancelled a stalled job, so from that point nothing was written to the log at all — the operator saw a job stuck on "running" with a dead log and no way to tell a working backup from a jammed daemon. Underneath, calls to the virtualisation service could wait forever: they have no time limit of their own, so if libvirt accepted a request and never answered, no amount of cancelling could free the backup, and even opening the connection could hang before anything was watching it. A run that stops making progress is now marked as stalled, with the reason, and that is published to the interface — so a stuck run can be told apart from a healthy one rather than both reading as "running". The run keeps its real status until it genuinely finishes, so nothing is reported as failed that has not actually failed. The watchdog also keeps reporting, at widening intervals, for as long as a cancelled run refuses to finish. Connecting to the virtualisation service is now time-limited, and a cancelled run still stuck on it after a grace period has its connection dropped so the stuck call fails and the run can finish. Dropping it can no longer strand a virtual machine: the shutdown-and-restart step disconnects that safety net first and reconnects if it has already fired, so the guest is still brought back up. Reported in #265.
  • Differential container backups no longer stop and restart containers that have nothing to back up. Every running container in the job was stopped and started again on each differential run, even when none of its folders had changed since the last full backup — pure downtime for no data. Vault now checks the folders first and leaves the container running when there is nothing new, applying the same exclusions as the backup itself so an excluded host-wide mount is never scanned. Full backups, containers marked not to be stopped, and containers that are already stopped all behave exactly as before.

  • Restoring a container to a chosen location no longer merges two of its folders into one. Where a restore sends data somewhere other than its original home, each folder lands in a directory named after the last part of its original path. Two folders whose paths differ only higher up — /mnt/user/app/config and /mnt/cache/other/config, say — therefore both claimed the same directory: their contents were interleaved, files with matching names overwrote one another, and the rebuilt container was pointed at that one directory for both. The clash is now detected before anything is written and the restore stops, naming both folders, rather than reporting success over merged data. Restoring to the original locations was never affected.

  • A restore no longer reports success when reloading a database dump failed part-way. The failure was written to the log and the restore finished normally, even though reloading a dump replaces the existing tables as it goes — so a reload that ran out of time, hit an error, or filled the disk left the database holding only part of its data while the restore said it had completed. Such a failure now fails the restore and says the database should not be relied on.

  • The daemon can no longer hang indefinitely while disconnecting from the virtualisation service. Closing a libvirt connection asked politely first and waited without limit for the answer, which never came if libvirtd had accepted the connection and then stopped responding — the exact situation the connection was meant to be able to break. Because the idle-check that runs before an adaptive backup holds the lock that serialises runs, one such hang stopped every later backup from starting. The polite close is now given five seconds before the connection is broken outright.

  • Restoring a container from a dedup destination to a custom location no longer writes volume data to the original paths while pointing the recreated container at the empty custom directory. The chunked restore path discarded the destination parameter and always wrote files back to the original bind sources, then recreated the container with mounts rewritten to the custom destination — so the running container was destroyed and replaced with one pointing at empty directories, while the data sat orphaned at the original paths. Volume data now lands under the custom destination (matching both the classic restore path and the container's rewritten binds), restoring parity between the two code paths. The classic restore path's volume-target computation is also extracted into a shared helper so the two can never drift apart again.

  • The Dashboard no longer contradicts itself on a fresh install. The Protected tile reported "All items covered" in green beside a red 0-of-N bar while every item was still waiting for its first backup — the caption counted only items missing from every job, and an item queued but never yet backed up is in neither group. It now reads how many are pending. The Health tile likewise announced "Attention needed — recent backups have not completed" on a server where nothing had failed and nothing had yet finished; a score of zero with no runs at all now reads "No backups completed yet".

docs.title: Security
docs.text: • Cleared a high-severity advisory in a build-time dependency and updated a bundled library. brace-expansion in the web UI's dependency tree is updated to a patched release (denial of service via unbounded expansion), and go.opentelemetry.io/otel moves to 1.44.0 for an unbounded-header-length advisory. Neither is reachable from Vault's own code and no runtime behaviour changes. A full vulnerability scan of the Go module graph and the web dependency tree reports nothing else outstanding.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The 8-Bit and 16-Bit themes now use fonts bundled with the plugin instead of downloading them from Google Fonts. Selecting a retro theme previously injected a stylesheet link to fonts.googleapis.com, so on a server without internet access — or behind a firewall or DNS filter that blocks Google — the pixel fonts silently fell back to Courier New and the theme lost its character. Press Start 2P and VT323 (both SIL OFL 1.1) now ship inside the web bundle and are served by the daemon itself, so every theme renders identically on an offline Unraid box and Vault makes no third-party network requests. The fonts are still fetched only when a retro theme is actually selected — the Default and 1-Bit themes download nothing.
  • Backup sizes in notifications now use sensible units instead of always megabytes. A completed-backup notification divided the total by a megabyte and printed it whatever the size, so a 2 TB backup arrived as "2097152.0 MB" — a number nobody can read at a glance. Sizes now pick their own unit, from bytes up to petabytes, in both the Unraid notification and the size and transfer speed in Discord messages. The code that turns a byte count into text had also been copied several times over and the copies had drifted apart, so the same 1.5 KB could read as "2 KB" in one place and "1.5 KB" in another. Notifications, backup progress, anomaly summaries, the main web console and the older plugin pages bundled with a release now share a single version of it. Some screens still have their own — the storage and recovery pages, the legacy history page, and the restore space check, which deliberately reports in KiB — and are unchanged here.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Cancelling a differential backup now takes effect immediately, even during the pre-scan of unchanged data. The changed_since pre-scan (pathChangedSince) walked a volume or VM disk tree to completion before honouring a cancel request, so cancelling a differential backup of a large, mostly-unchanged path could hang until the whole tree had been read. The scan now checks for cancellation between files — matching the rest of the backup engine — so container (classic and dedup/chunked) and VM differential backups stop promptly. As part of making cancellation prompt: a cancelled container backup now always restarts the container it stopped (the restart no longer rides on the cancelled request context, which previously could leave a running container stopped), and an operator Cancel is no longer occasionally misclassified as a stall and scheduled for an automatic retry. Closes #251.
  • Differential backups of containers that bind-mount the host root no longer scan the entire host filesystem before skipping it. On the classic (tar) path the changed_since pre-scan ran before the mount-exclusion check, so a differential backup of a container mounting / (Telegraf, Netdata, Glances, cAdvisor, node-exporter) walked all of / only to then discard it — the same runaway walk originally fixed in #70. The exclusion check now runs first, matching the dedup/chunked path.
  • Container backups to dedup/chunked destinations now stop the container first for a consistent snapshot. The chunked/dedup backup path read container volumes live without stopping the container, unlike the classic tar path which stops running containers (unless Don't stop is set). In-flight writes during the copy could produce an inconsistent or corrupt dedup backup. The chunked path now mirrors the classic behaviour: it honours the no_stop setting, stops a running container before reading its volumes, and guarantees the container is restarted afterwards — even if the backup fails partway through.
  • Differential backups to dedup/chunked destinations now skip unchanged data at the filesystem level. The chunked/dedup backup path did not honour the changed_since reference that the classic tar path already used, so an incremental run re-read and re-processed files (and whole container volumes) that had not changed since the last backup. Files and volumes older than the reference are now skipped in the chunked walk — matching the differential behaviour of the tar path — while directories are still recorded. A malformed or absent changed_since safely falls back to a full backup. Closes #249.
  • The web UI no longer hangs forever on the loading spinner in Brave (and other privacy-hardened browsers). Brave's default Shields can make localStorage and matchMedia throw a SecurityError — most often when the console is embedded in the Unraid page as an iframe — which aborted theme setup during boot before the app ever became interactive, so the tab loaded endlessly ("Tab is not responding"). Every storage/media-query access during startup is now guarded and degrades to sensible in-memory defaults, and a boot watchdog guarantees the interface always becomes usable even if a startup step stalls. Closes #250.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• A connection banner now appears when the live link to the Vault daemon is lost. Instead of a silently frozen page, a banner explains that data may be out of date and offers a one-click reload, so a persistent connection problem is visible and recoverable rather than invisible.
  • The live-update WebSocket now reconnects with exponential backoff and jitter (capped at 30s) instead of a fixed 3-second loop, so an unreachable daemon no longer churns the network and many clients reconnecting after a restart don't stampede in lockstep.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Direct LAN access to the daemon now answers browser Private Network Access preflights. Chrome and Brave (130+/Edge 143+) block requests from a more-public origin to a private LAN/loopback address unless the daemon echoes Access-Control-Allow-Private-Network: true on the preflight. The daemon now returns this header alongside its existing CORS response, without changing the origin allow-list, so the Unraid-embedded and LAN-IP access paths keep working across browsers.

  • Cleared three high-severity advisories in build-time dependencies. brace-expansion (reachable through ESLint) is updated to a patched release in the web UI's dependency tree. The repository root also carried a second, unused npm project whose only declared dependency was the shadcn CLI — it was referenced nowhere, excluded from every build, yet still accumulated advisories (brace-expansion, js-yaml) that had to be patched. It has been removed rather than patched again. None of these packages ship in the daemon or the web UI, so no runtime behaviour changes.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • Changing the database location now reports whether the database actually moved. Saving a new location previously confirmed only "Snapshot path updated", which said nothing about the data itself. Settings now reports the migration — for example "Database migrated to /mnt/garbage/vault.db — 5 files removed from /mnt/cache/.vault/vault.db" — and if the move could not be completed it says so as an error, naming the reason, so it is clear the database is still readable at its previous location.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • The directory browser no longer opens empty when the field holds a file path. The Database Location field stores a file (vault.db), which the browse API rejects, so opening the browser from it silently failed and showed a blank dialog with no way to navigate. The browser now falls back to the containing directory — and to the top-level listing if that also fails — so it always opens somewhere usable.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Browsing for a Database Location or Temporary Work Area no longer applies the change on its own. Confirming a folder in the directory browser saved and applied it immediately, while typing the same path required clicking Apply — so the two ways of setting the field behaved differently, and picking a folder could move the database before you had a chance to review it. Browsing now only fills the field; Apply commits it in both cases.
  • Changing the database location now moves the database instead of copying it. Pointing Vault at a custom location (or reverting to the default) previously wrote a fresh copy at the new path but left the old one behind, so a stale vault.db — plus its rotated copies — stayed on the previous drive indefinitely. Because startup picks the freshest valid database across all known locations, that leftover was not merely untidy: if the new drive was ever slow to mount (a ZFS pool importing after the cache pool, for example), the old copy could be selected and silently undo the move. The previous location is now retired once the new one is confirmed written, so nothing is left to go stale. Only Vault's own files are removed — a custom location that is a share or pool root keeps everything else in it untouched, and the old copy is always left in place if the new one did not write successfully.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• The web UI no longer keeps running the old version after a plugin upgrade. index.html was served with no cache headers at all, so browsers applied their own heuristic caching and could keep loading the previous JavaScript bundle against the freshly-upgraded API until the user manually hard-refreshed. index.html is now explicitly never cached, while the content-hashed assets under /assets/ are cached permanently (they can never change identity), so upgrades take effect on the next normal page load.
  • Deleting a storage destination that jobs still use no longer leaves those jobs silently broken. Confirming the deletion previously removed the destination but left every dependent job enabled and pointing at an id that no longer existed — the Jobs page showed the destination as "Unknown" and the scheduler kept starting runs that could never write anywhere. Dependent jobs are now disabled and their destination cleared, and the response reports how many were affected so the UI can tell you what to re-point.
  • Creating or editing a job with a storage destination that doesn't exist now explains the problem instead of failing with a generic "internal server error" (HTTP 500). The invalid reference is reported as a normal validation error naming the offending id.
  • Job settings are validated before they are saved. Unrecognised values for backup type, compression, encryption, container/VM mode, verification mode and notification trigger — plus negative retention counts, out-of-range retry overrides and excessively long job names — were previously accepted and stored, only surfacing later as a confusing failure mid-backup. They are now rejected with a message naming the field and its allowed values. (Upload concurrency continues to be clamped rather than rejected, as before.)
  • "Test Connection" against an unreachable host now reports the failure instead of returning nothing. When a remote host silently dropped packets, the connectivity probe and the server's response deadline expired at the same instant, so the error could never be sent and the browser saw an empty reply after a 15-second wait. Probes now finish early enough for the error to be delivered — a blackholed replication target reports a clear timeout error in about 10 seconds.
  • Dashboard protection counts no longer double-count items that belong to more than one job. A VM or container covered by two jobs was counted once per job, inflating the totals; and when only one of those jobs had produced a restore point the same item was reported as both "protected" and "pending" at once. Items are now counted once, and an item backed up by any job counts as protected.
  • Size anomaly messages no longer contradict their own numbers. A run marginally smaller than usual could be described as "This backup grew to 2.7 GB, about <1× its usual 2.8 GB". The wording now follows the actual direction of the change.
  • Restore item-type filters are labelled properly — the ZFS filter read "zfss" and virtual machines read "vms"; they now read "ZFS Datasets" and "VMs".
  • Jobs, Restore, and History stay responsive with production-scale data. The pages now hydrate job items, anomaly baselines, and run history through bounded bulk queries instead of issuing hundreds of browser requests; bulk queries are cancellation-aware and indexed for deterministic newest-first history.
  • Replica mode no longer requests daemon-only discovery APIs or exposes daemon-only pages through direct links. Jobs, Restore, Recovery, and Recover Vault now redirect to Dashboard on a replica, matching the hidden navigation and read-only API contract.
  • Custom folder jobs can no longer bypass the server's allowed-root policy by typing or crafting a path. Create and update validate settings.path and legacy path fields against the same /mnt, /boot, and discovered-ZFS boundary used by the browser, while retaining overlap protection against backing up into the destination itself.
  • Recovery readiness now counts configured items consistently when discovery is unavailable. Duplicate items are counted once, custom folders remain tracked, Flash Drive follows its own setting, and the page no longer shows a false empty state beside a non-zero protected count.

  • Historical anomaly messages with the old “grew … <1×” contradiction now render correctly in both Anomalies and Activity Log without rewriting stored audit history.

  • Very large VM backups to Hetzner Storage Box (WebDAV) no longer fail on the final metadata write (closes #242). Hetzner answers a WebDAV "create directory" request for a directory that already exists with 403 instead of the standard 405, which made the very last, tiny file of a multi-hour VM upload fail and discard the entire finished backup. Vault now recognises this reply (and any other non-standard status) by verifying that the directory actually exists, and treats it as success. Long VM copies also log a progress milestone every 5 minutes (percent, bytes, elapsed time), so a failure hours into a large backup is finally diagnosable from the diagnostics bundle.

  • Folder backups of cache-only shares no longer produce empty archives. On Unraid a cache-only share appears under /mnt/user/ as a symlink to /mnt/cache/, and the backup walk did not follow it — it saw a symlink rather than a directory, never descended, and wrote an archive containing nothing. Both the classic tar and dedup paths now resolve the source symlink before walking, so the share's real contents are captured. The recorded restore location still uses the path you configured (e.g. /mnt/user/myshare), not the internal cache target, so restores land where you expect.
  • Configuration — including the Temporary Work Area path — no longer reverts to an old state after a server reboot (closes #241). Two root causes fixed: (1) on boot Vault now restores the freshest valid database copy by comparing modification times across all persistence locations — including the USB-direct database written when a boot ran before the cache pool was mounted, which the old fixed-order chain never even considered, so newer settings were silently overwritten by a stale cache snapshot; (2) the plugin now installs Unraid event hooks: stopping_svcs stops the daemon gracefully on reboot/array-stop so the final database flush gets the chance to complete before the OS kills processes, and started starts the daemon after the array is up if the boot-time start raced the pool mount.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: • Storage adapters now contain symlinks to the destination root. A symlink planted under a local destination can no longer redirect reads, listings, or deletes outside the configured base path (resolved-to-resolved comparison, so destinations that legitimately live behind symlinks like /mnt/user fuse paths keep working). SFTP destinations get the same server-side check (via realpath) on the browse/download surface. S3 has no symlinks; SMB/NFS client libraries offer no resolution primitive and follow their server's own symlink policy.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Very large VM backups (100 GB+) no longer fail or destabilise the daemon (closes #239). The VM engine's fixed 2-hour wall-clock limit is replaced by a progress-resetting 30-minute idle timeout, so a huge disk that is still copying can run for as long as it needs — only a genuinely stalled job is aborted, and Vault now attempts (with retries and verification) to abort the in-flight libvirt job on stall or cancellation so the hypervisor stops writing into the staging area. Full VM backups check staging free space up front and fail fast with an actionable message instead of dying mid-copy, and background worker panics (uploads, downloads, health checks, async cleanups) are contained as failed runs instead of crashing the whole daemon.

  • Restoring an incremental/differential folder backup no longer resurrects deleted or excluded files (closes #231). Folder backups now record an authoritative point-in-time file listing alongside each restore point; after replaying the chain, the restore prunes files that earlier chain steps wrote but that no longer existed (or were excluded) at the selected point. Dedup folder restore points restore directly from their complete manifest — no chain replay at all, which also makes them faster. The restore wizard's file picker reflects the same rules, so it only offers files a restore will actually produce. Backups made before this version have no listing and keep the old overlay behavior.

  • Running and queued backups can now actually be cancelled from the UI (closes #235, closes #238). The documented Cancel flow never had a button: the Jobs page now shows a Cancel control on the running/queued job's row, and the Dashboard's "Backup in progress" tile has a Cancel button with live "Cancelling…" state. Cancelling a job that is queued behind another run (e.g. Run Now on a scheduled job while a backup is active) removes it from the queue before it starts — previously such runs could not be stopped at all. Deleting a running job now cancels its run first instead of leaving the backup goroutine running against deleted records.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Adaptive backups — jobs can wait for their workloads to go idle (closes #240). A new per-job "Adaptive Backup" toggle checks each container's CPU/network activity (Docker stats), each VM's CPU activity (libvirt), and each folder's recent writes before a scheduled run starts. Busy workloads (Plex mid-stream, a download still writing) postpone the backup with a clear reason in History (new postponed status), re-checking every few minutes until idle — or until a configurable max-postpone window elapses, when the backup runs anyway so busy systems still get protected. Manual Run Now always runs immediately. Idle thresholds and windows are configurable in the global settings; probe failures never block a backup (fail-open).

  • Local destinations can now be throttled too (#237 follow-up). The per-destination bandwidth cap — previously hidden for local storage — now appears as a "Disk write speed limit" on local destinations, capping how fast backups write to disk so apps streaming from the same array (Plex, Jellyfin) keep their I/O headroom while a backup runs. The cap is write-only: restores and verification always read at full speed. Note the unit is megabits (8 Mbps = 1 MB/s). The cap applies to the copy-to-destination phase; keep staging on a different disk (cache, the default) for full effect.

  • Adaptive upload throttling — Vault now yields bandwidth to Plex, Jellyfin and friends (closes #237). An opt-in "Upload Throttling" section in Settings lets you enter your link's upload capacity; Vault then continuously measures non-Vault traffic on the network interface and slows its own uploads to network destinations so streaming keeps its bandwidth, speeding back up when the link goes quiet. A configurable minimum rate keeps backups progressing, per-destination bandwidth caps still apply (stricter limit wins), and changes take effect within seconds without a restart.
  • Browse the files on a storage destination like an FTP client (closes #236). Each destination card on the Storage page now has a Browse button that opens a read-only file browser — drill into folders with breadcrumb navigation and see file sizes and modification times for whatever Vault sees on the destination (local, SFTP, SMB, NFS, WebDAV, S3). Available in replica mode too since it never writes anything.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The Replication and Storage Logging toggles in Settings now apply immediately — flipping the switch saves right away (rolling back with an error toast if the save fails), so the separate "Save Replication Settings" and "Save" buttons are gone.
  • The Full Form "sensible defaults" note in the job editor is now a prominent info callout instead of small dim text, so it's clear why Advanced Options are not shown in Full Form mode (closes #232).
  • Documentation is now linked directly from the sidebar — a new "Documentation" entry in the System section opens the Vault manual in a new tab (closes #233).
  • Backup type docs and job editor now explain first-run behavior: selecting Incremental or Differential on a new job automatically performs a Full backup on the first run, so no manual initial Full is needed. Clarified in the manual, the API reference, the backup_type_chain field description, and the job editor's helper text (closes #234).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Restoring an incremental or differential backup no longer sends duplicate "Restore completed" notifications. The runner notified once per chain step (base full + each increment), so a single folder restore could produce several identical Unraid notifications — some arriving while the restore was still running. One notification is now sent per restored item, after the whole chain has been replayed.
  • The restore wizard's file picker now works on incremental and differential restore points. Browsing a restore point only listed the files captured by that specific increment — often nothing, showing an empty "No files match" picker even though a restore would recover the full folder. The picker now merges the file lists of the entire backup chain (base full plus increments, newest version of each file winning), matching what a restore actually produces.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • Folder backups now honor the exclude_paths setting (#230). The runner never passed a folder item's configured exclusions to the backup engine, so exclusion patterns (e.g. *.log or a logs directory) were silently ignored and excluded files still ended up in folder backups. Exclusions now apply to both classic tar and dedup/chunked folder backups, matching the container behavior. Note: exclusions added to an existing incremental/differential chain take full effect from the next full backup (#231). Thanks to @0x1917 for the fix and regression tests!

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • Bind address and port changes now actually restart the daemon (Settings → Vault → Apply). The plugin package shipped apply.sh without execute permission, so Unraid's settings-save hook failed with a silent "Permission denied" and the daemon kept running on its previous address. Selecting a NIC address (e.g. 192.168.20.21) then made the web UI report Vault daemon unavailable while Start insisted it was already running, because the daemon was still bound to 127.0.0.1. The package now ships apply.sh executable and the installer re-applies the permission on every install/upgrade, healing existing installs.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Recover Vault wizard — guided disaster recovery after a server rebuild (closes #220). A fresh install now offers a clear choice — Set up Vault or Recover from a backup — and the new five-step wizard walks you through reconnecting your backup storage, entering your backup password, restoring the Vault database (jobs, storage, history, settings), and fixing folder paths that changed on the rebuilt server. Also reachable any time from Recovery → Recover Vault.
  • Database restore now works with encrypted backups. POST /api/v1/storage/{id}/restore-db restores the encrypted vault.db.latest.age snapshots Vault writes by default (previously only a plaintext vault.db could be restored), verifies your backup password before touching anything (verify_only), re-seals the password with the new server's key so scheduled DB backups stay encrypted after recovery, and reloads the database in-process — no daemon restart needed after a restore.
  • GET /api/v1/storage/{id}/db-backups lists the database snapshots available on a destination (newest first, with the latest pointer flagged).
  • Path check after recovery: GET /api/v1/recovery/path-audit flags folder and local-storage paths from the restored config that don't exist on this server, and POST /api/v1/recovery/path-remap updates them in place — the exact "my array and shares are different now" pain from #220.
  • Disaster Recovery guide in the docs — including why hand-copying vault.db to the flash drive doesn't work and what to do instead.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • Vault's own database now reliably runs in WAL mode with a 30-second lock timeout. The SQLite driver was silently ignoring the connection options that were meant to set these, so freshly created databases ran in rollback-journal mode with no busy timeout — slower under concurrent access and more prone to "database is locked" errors. All connection settings are now applied in a form the driver understands, and Vault logs a warning if WAL is unavailable on the filesystem.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: • Snapshot rotation and database-backup temp-file cleanup now refuse to delete any path that isn't absolute and traversal-free — hardening flagged by CodeQL; no user-visible behavior change.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Dashboard is now uncluttered on a fresh install. Until you've configured storage and your first backup job, the dashboard shows just the Getting Started guide plus the four at-a-glance KPI tiles (Health, Protected, Next Run, Last Backup). The heavier panels — Backup Jobs, Protection status, Recent Activity, 3-2-1 rule, and the storage/analytics tiles — stay hidden until there's real data to fill them, so they no longer render empty. They appear automatically once your first job exists.
  • Documentation screenshots refreshed to match the current Vault dashboard, storage, job wizard, recovery, responsive, and theme-aware UI.
  • License changed from MIT to AGPL-3.0. Vault is now distributed under the GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 to keep derivative and network-served modifications open source.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• VM backup jobs now detect raw vs qcow2 disks and only offer supported backup types (closes #163). Vault reads each VM's disk format at discovery time and exposes it (disk_format, supports_incremental) on GET /api/v1/vms. Because libvirt checkpoint-based incremental/differential backups require qcow2 disks, the job wizard now hides those options — and falls back to Full — when a selected VM uses raw or mixed disks, with an inline note naming the affected VM. This surfaces up front the constraint the engine previously enforced silently by downgrading raw-disk VMs to full backups.
  • Pre/post-backup scripts now receive job context as environment variables (part of #187). The job editor has long promised VAULT_JOB_NAME and VAULT_STATUS to hook scripts, but they were never actually set. Vault now exports VAULT_JOB_NAME, VAULT_STATUS (starting for pre-scripts, the run's final status for post-scripts), VAULT_JOB_ID, and VAULT_RUN_ID into every pre/post-backup script's environment — enabling, for example, an Immich pg_dump pre-script that targets the right job.
  • Container exclusion presets can now carry advisory notes and warnings (part of #187). GET /api/v1/presets/exclusions returns optional notes/warnings for apps that need a caveat, and the job wizard shows them inline beneath the container's exclusions.
  • Docker named volumes are now backed up, not silently skipped. Vault previously only backed up bind mounts, so containers that store their data in named docker volumes (many compose stacks — the single most-reported gap for the old appdata.backup plugin) were archived empty. Vault now backs up named volume mounts too — a volume's data lives at a real host path (/var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/_data), handled exactly like a bind mount — across the classic, dedup and restore paths, and reattaches them on restore via the container's bind spec. The job wizard's mount editor lists them tagged "named volume" so you can include or exclude each one. Anonymous volumes (a random 64-hex id) are deliberately skipped because they can't be reliably reattached on restore; tmpfs/npipe and other non-data mounts are skipped as before.
  • Compression level is now configurable per job (fastest / default / better / best). The job wizard exposes a level next to the compression algorithm, mapped to the zstd/gzip encoder levels, so you can trade backup time for archive size. The default level is unchanged, so existing jobs and their archives are byte-for-byte identical.
  • Jobs that would back up into their own source are now rejected up front. Saving a job whose local destination path sits inside (or contains) one of its folder/flash source trees now returns a clear error instead of silently archiving each run into the next run's source — the old plugin's "backing itself up" footgun. Remote destinations are unaffected.
  • Sparse files that could stall a backup are now flagged. Vault logs a warning when a large file's logical size vastly exceeds its on-disk size (e.g. a Meilisearch/LMDB store reporting terabytes but occupying kilobytes), so a slow backup reading the full logical extent is no longer a silent mystery — the exact trap behind the old plugin's multi-hour stalls.
  • Containers that route their network through another container are flagged. When a container uses network_mode: container:<other> (a Gluetun/VPN-sidecar setup), Vault now logs a note reminding you to include the provider in the same job and order it to start first, so the dependent doesn't lose its network when restarted after backup.
  • The Command Palette (⌘K) now finds backup items and restore points, not just pages (closes #210). Typing a container, VM, or folder name surfaces it under an Items group and jumps straight to its restore view in one action; each job's most recent restore point is listed under Restore Points. Results are grouped (Pages / Items / Restore Points / Jobs / Storage) and loaded once when the palette opens, so filtering stays instant.
  • Storage destinations can now be tested before saving (part of #206). The add/edit modal has a prominent Test connection button that validates the current form — including S3 credentials and endpoints — against the backend before you commit the destination, with clear pending / success / failure states. Backed by a new POST /api/v1/storage/test endpoint that builds an ephemeral adapter from the posted config.
  • Two more Dashboard tiles — Retention & cleanup and Replication status (Dashboard polish). Retention & cleanup shows how many restore points a job's long-term-retention policy would prune next, out of the total, plus when the next prune runs; Replication status rolls up offsite sync state across replication sources (synced count and most recent last-synced time, red when any source failed). Both draw from data already on the page, appear in the Customize catalog, and hide automatically when no job has a retention policy / no replication source is configured.
  • Redesigned, customizable Dashboard (Dashboard "5A" + E13). The Dashboard now leads with a status hero — Health, Protected (X/Y + bar), Next run countdown, and Last backup result — so "am I protected right now?" is answered above the fold, followed by a live Backup in progress / Recent activity / Backup jobs / Protection status grid. Every tile is drawn from data already on the page (no new endpoints). Info tiles are click-through — Next run → Jobs, Last backup / Health / Success rate → History, Storage → Storage, and so on. A Customize mode lets you add, remove, and reorder tiles (drag on desktop, ↑/↓ buttons for keyboard and touch) from a catalog that also includes Storage (combined & per-target), Recovery readiness, Needs attention, Success rate, Anomalies, Quick actions, Backup size trend, Backup calendar heatmap, Dedup & compression savings, Storage forecast ("full in ~N days"), and Largest backups — each drawn from data already available (history trend, dedup stats, capacity trajectory) and loaded lazily only when the tile is added; Tiles are resizable in Customize mode (narrower/wider steps across the 12-col grid), size to their content, and compact vertically — each tile packs upward into the space a shorter neighbour would otherwise leave beside a taller one, so the grid stays tidy with no holes between tiles (a fixed-grid-with-compaction model, as used by Grafana/Datadog/gridstack, rather than Pinterest-style masonry which reorders unpredictably when the layout or screen size changes). The layout and per-tile widths persist per-browser (vault:dash:layout:v1) and Reset restores the default. Every tile now follows one compact, data-dense layout — an icon-chip header with an uppercase label, a large tabular-figure value, and a micro-visual (progress/usage bar, sparkline, dedup ratio, or the contribution-style calendar heatmap) — for a consistent, professional ops-dashboard look in light, dark, and retro themes. On phones the small KPI tiles sit two-up (single column only below 360px). The 12-column grid reflows to 2-up tiles and full-width panels on tablets and phones (single column on very small screens), and works in light, dark, and all three retro themes. The Create Job wizard now offers a Switch to full form toggle that renders every primary field on one scrollable page for users who create jobs often; advanced settings keep their defaults and stay available in the step-by-step view.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Dashboard polish — accessibility and correctness. Added an app-wide prefers-reduced-motion guard so motion-sensitive users no longer get the live-progress pulse, progress-bar shimmer, run spinners, or the long health-ring/bar transitions (only a handful of named animations were previously covered). Compact KPI tiles (Health, Protected, Next run, Success rate, Needs attention, and the like) can no longer be stretched to full width in Customize mode — a per-tile width cap keeps a single figure from becoming an awkward full-width band, and any width persisted beyond the cap is clamped on load; wide panels (Jobs, Activity, Calendar, Size trend, Largest) still reach full width. On phones the narrower/wider resize arrows are hidden in Customize mode — the grid is forced to 1–2 columns there, so tapping them changed nothing — while reorder (↑/↓) and remove (×) still work. Essential KPI captions moved from the faint text-dim to text-muted for WCAG-AA contrast in light mode, and the Health tile gained a "View backup history" tooltip clarifying where it navigates.
  • Replica (read-only) instances no longer show write actions they can't perform. In replica mode the Dashboard (run-all, quick actions, per-item restore, 3-2-1 dismiss), Storage (add/edit/delete/import/DB-backup/cleanup/breaker), Replication (add/edit/delete/sync), Anomalies (ack/dismiss), History (purge), and the destructive/secret Settings controls (API key, encryption, snapshot path) are now hidden behind a "Read-only replica" notice, instead of surfacing buttons that only fail against the server's read-only guard.
  • Duplicating a backup job no longer opens an unsaveable form. Duplicate now carries the original job's backup type(s) across (it previously copied the items but not the type selection), so the wizard doesn't strand you on an invalid first step. Inline job rename also no longer fires twice when you press Enter and then blur.
  • Recovery readiness copy now matches the ring, and the Restore banner tells the truth about where data lands. The readiness summary follows the ring's colour bands (red under 50%, amber 50–99%, green only at 100%), an empty setup reads "No items to protect yet" instead of a false 100%, and the unprotected list now includes folders/flash so it matches the count. The restore overwrite banner shows a concrete path only when it's actually known (custom destination, or a folder/flash item) and says "its original location" for containers/VMs rather than a hard-coded /mnt/user/appdata/... that could be wrong.
  • Assorted UI robustness fixes. partial/pending backup runs now render amber consistently (Dashboard, History) instead of red/grey; the storage connection test can't show a stale "Connection OK" if you edit the form mid-test; the Settings "Database" jump link is hidden when that section isn't shown; the Dashboard protection bar turns green only when every item is truly protected; API requests now time out after 15s and report expired auth clearly; and Storage/History surface a load error instead of a falsely-empty "all clear" when their initial fetch fails.
  • Express-mode job creation no longer submits invalid forms via Enter key. The Jobs page form submit handler now applies the same canSaveExpress gate as the disabled Save buttons, so pressing Enter in an input cannot bypass required item/storage/name validation.
  • The Dashboard "Next run" now shows the real countdown again. The /jobs/next-runs (and /jobs/{id}/next-run) endpoints returned empty because the API router — and its job handler — is built in NewServer, before the daemon wires the scheduler's next-run resolver, so the handler captured a nil resolver and every job reported "not scheduled". The resolver is now propagated to the already-registered handler when it's set, so scheduled jobs report their next run correctly.
  • Backups no longer fail when the Recycle Bin plugin is installed (closes #204). The Unraid Recycle Bin plugin creates a /mnt/RecycleBin view directory (symlinks/subfolders, not a real pool) that it rebuilds periodically. Vault's staging-pool discovery treated it as a normal pool and staged backups there, so a docker or flash backup could fail mid-run with open /mnt/RecycleBin/.vault-stage/…: no such file or directory when the plugin regenerated the view. /mnt/RecycleBin (and any dot-prefixed /mnt entry such as a stray .Recycle.Bin) is now excluded from staging-pool candidates.
  • Flash and folder backups now honour path exclusions (closes #204). The classic tar backup path used for flash/folder items on non-dedup destinations ignored exclude_paths entirely, and the job wizard offered no way to set them. Folder items (including the Flash Drive preset) now have an "Exclude paths" editor in the wizard's advanced step, and the engine applies those exclusions on the classic path just as it already did for deduplicated backups — so you can, for example, exclude a share's .Recycle.Bin folder from a flash backup.
  • The Recycle Bin plugin's trash folder is auto-excluded from the Flash Drive backup when detected (closes #204).
